mechanics.body_shape: the prologue saves ESI and aliases the receiver into it, one unconditional direct call runs, bit 0 of the single argument is tested, a conditional second direct call runs with the receiver pushed, EAX is materialised from the alias on both paths, ESI is restored and the epilogue pops 4 bytes
mechanics.frame_arithmetic_at_0x0067dc88: On entry ESP points at the return address and the argument is at ESP+4. PUSH ESI at 0x0067dc80 puts the saved register at ESP+0 and the return address at ESP+4. The CALL at 0x0067dc83 puts its return address at ESP+0, so the saved register is at ESP+4 and the argument is at ESP+8. The CALL has returned by the time the TEST runs, so the argument is at ESP+8. The tested word is therefore the argument and neither the saved register nor the return address.

unresolved_questions: Why does the record name this body 'App::IMessageManager::Get'? The image shows a scalar deleting destructor at vtable slot 0 and nothing that reads like a getter. Either the SDK name is wrong, or the slot-0 destructor and the 'Get' are two different things the symbol table has conflated, and this body is only one of them. The bridge returns no sibling App::IMessageManager symbol, so the symbol table cannot settle it and no runtime observation of this target exists.

Who dispatches this body, and with what argument? fan_in is 0, callers is [], and the only reference to the address is the vtable entry at 0x01401798. So the entry conditions under which bit 0 of the argument is set are not established by anything in this repository -- which matters, because the whole difference between the two paths in this body is that bit.

Is the value this body returns safe to use on the path where it just released the receiver? The body releases the receiver at 0x00f47380 and then returns that same receiver at 0x0067dc98. Whether 0x00f47380 tolerates being called on an object whose destructor has already run, and whether the returned word is meant to be discarded, is not established by any record for this target.

Why does 0x0067db10 test the flag at [ESI+0x11] before releasing the members at [ESI+0x14] and [ESI+0x20]? That gating lives in the callee, not here, and this package claims nothing about what it means. It is recorded because it is the only other place in the immediate neighbourhood where a 'should I tear down' flag is consulted, and a reader comparing the two bodies will want to know that the question was seen and not answered.

What are the receiver's members? Nothing in any record for this target names one, and this body reads none. The header's port types are void for that reason alone, and the model declares no offset, so the question is open rather than answered by omission.

The argument's upper 24 bits: this body reads one byte and masks one bit. Whether a caller ever puts anything but 0 or 1 in the other three bytes is not observable from this body and is not claimed either way.

behaviourally_indistinguishable_mutation: Returning the receiver through a different local, or writing receiver + 0 explicitly: the same value reaches EAX by any route, so no test on the returned word can separate them. The claim is about the value, not about the instruction that moves it.

A store into the receiver that writes back the value it had just read would leave every byte identical and would pass test_no_byte_of_the_receiver_is_read_or_written. This is stated in the test itself. No store is claimed to be excluded on that ground; every store that changes a byte is excluded, and the body is not claimed to store at all.

Reordering the two release-block statements in a way that still pushes and calls once with the same pointer is indistinguishable, because the listing fixes no order between PUSH ESI at 0x0067dc8f and the CALL at 0x0067dc90 other than push-then-call, which the model keeps.

Emitting the receiver copy after the first call instead of before it is indistinguishable through this interface, because the callee is an observer that cannot write to the caller's argument. The listing places MOV ESI,ECX at 0x0067dc81 before the call, and the model matches it, but the test cannot tell the two apart and does not claim to.

The envelope abstained deliberately: receiver_not_determinable / ecx_read_without_deref, because __thiscall and __fastcall both put the first operand in ECX and nothing in the two entry bytes separates them. This package's __thiscall is not the envelope's guess; it is fixed by both callees' own listings plus this body's own RET 0x4, all cited under observed_original_abi.
